REFERRAL REASON
Microsatellite instability (MSI) analysis requested for colorectal adenocarcinoma from right hemicolectomy specimen. Patient meets BETHESDA criteria for Lynch Syndrome screening based on family history.

CLINICAL INFORMATION
Diagnosis: Colorectal adenocarcinoma, right colon
Specimen Type: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue and matched blood sample
Tumor Content: 50% neoplastic cell nuclei
Family History: Meets BETHESDA criteria for hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome evaluation

METHODOLOGY
Microsatellite Instability (MSI) Analysis by PCR
Test performed using GeneScan MSI Detection Kit for analysis of five mononucleotide microsatellite markers. DNA was extracted from microdissected tumor tissue (50% neoplastic nuclei) and matched peripheral blood leukocytes. PCR amplification was performed for the following microsatellite loci: BAT-25, BAT-26, NR-21, NR-24, and MONO-27. Fragment analysis was performed by capillary electrophoresis with comparison of tumor and normal DNA profiles.

RESULTS

Microsatellite Instability Analysis:
BAT-25: UNSTABLE - shift detected in tumor DNA
BAT-26: UNSTABLE - shift detected in tumor DNA
NR-21: UNSTABLE - shift detected in tumor DNA
NR-24: STABLE - no shift detected
MONO-27: UNSTABLE - shift detected in tumor DNA

Result: HIGH MICROSATELLITE INSTABILITY (MSI-H)
4 of 5 microsatellite markers demonstrate instability

TECHNICAL NOTE
Microsatellite instability is defined as a change in the number of short tandem DNA repeats in tumor tissue compared to normal tissue from the same individual. MSI-H is defined as instability in ≥2 of 5 markers (or ≥30% of markers tested). This phenotype is characteristic of tumors with defective DNA mismatch repair.

SUMMARY AND INTERPRETATION
This colorectal adenocarcinoma demonstrates high microsatellite instability (MSI-H), with 4 of 5 tested markers showing instability. MSI-H is indicative of a defect in the DNA mismatch repair system and is found in approximately 15% of colorectal carcinomas. In the context of this patient meeting BETHESDA criteria, this finding raises strong suspicion for Lynch Syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer syndrome).

MSI-H tumors may arise through either:
1. Germline mutations in mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) - Lynch Syndrome
2. Somatic hypermethylation of the MLH1 promoter - sporadic MSI-H colorectal cancer

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing on tumor DNA to distinguish between Lynch Syndrome and sporadic MSI-H colorectal cancer
2. If MLH1 promoter hypermethylation is absent, proceed with:
   - Immunohistochemistry for mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2)
   - Germline genetic testing for Lynch Syndrome genes
3. Genetic counseling for the patient and at-risk family members
4. Enhanced surveillance protocols if Lynch Syndrome is confirmed

This test was developed and its performance characteristics determined by [redacted location] Medical Center Molecular Genetics Laboratory. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

[redacted name], MD, PhD
Director, Molecular Genetics Laboratory
